findings.proof: bin/greet.sh:9 passes the user's name to echo; under dash (/bin/sh on Debian/Ubuntu) `greet.sh 'a\tb'` now prints a real tab, and `greet.sh 'x\c'` prints `hello x` with no newline. Before this change printf printed both literally.
findings.claim: Swapping printf for echo makes /bin/sh read backslash escapes in the name, so names with a backslash print wrong even without --shout.
findings.suggestion:
Print with printf and skip the captured variable. This also keeps trailing newlines that $(...) would strip:
if [ "${shout}" = yes ]; then
  printf 'hello %s\n' "${name}" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]'
else
  printf 'hello %s\n' "${name}"
fi

findings.claim: `tr a-z A-Z` only uppercases ASCII, so `--shout é` prints `HELLO é` (shellcheck SC2018/SC2019).

noticed.text: The comment's "--shout first prints it in capitals" reads as if it prints twice. Something like "with --shout as the first argument, prints it in capitals" is clearer.
There is no test for --shout. The only test checks the plain greeting.

notes.text: Under set -eu, the --shout check on the left of && does not abort the script when it is false, and ${1-} means it is safe with no arguments.
The script uses only POSIX sh features, which fits its #!/bin/sh shebang.
